content:
This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in nosql modeling work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Prefer explicit, readable nosql modeling solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
2. Keep nosql modeling outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
3. State assumptions about nosql modeling explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
4. Re-check edge cases relevant to nosql modeling (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
5. Before starting nosql modeling work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
6. Measure before optimizing any nosql modeling bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. When multiple nosql modeling strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. Prefer the simplest nosql modeling approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
9. Validate nosql modeling outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
10. Keep nosql modeling changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
11. Surface known limitations of a chosen nosql modeling approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
12. Check that nosql modeling terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting nosql modeling assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Avoid introducing new nosql modeling abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Avoid mixing unrelated nosql modeling concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not apply generic nosql modeling advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about nosql modeling over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
